title: Anzac Biscuits
subtitle: golden syrup and oat biscuits from Australian and New Zealand tradition
excerpt: Anzac biscuits are chewy, golden oat biscuits sweetened with golden syrup and packed with coconut. They contain no eggs, which made them suitable for sending overseas in wartime. They keep exceptionally well and improve in a tin.
sourceNotes: An Australian and New Zealand classic associated with the Anzac soldiers of the First World War. Made by families and sent abroad.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked biscuits. Defrost at room temperature.
recipe.batchNotes: Double easily. They keep for 2 weeks in an airtight tin.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps very well. Make a batch at the start of the week.
recipe.temperatureNote: Conventional oven -- low heat gives chewy biscuits; higher heat gives crunchier ones

content.text: The baking soda goes in last, dissolved in boiling water and added to the hot syrup mixture -- this causes it to foam up and creates a light texture. Work quickly once it goes in, as the reaction is brief.
Heat the oven to 160C. Line two baking sheets.
Combine the oats, flour, caster sugar, and desiccated coconut in a large bowl.
Melt the butter and golden syrup together in a saucepan. Dissolve the bicarbonate of soda in 2 tbsp boiling water and add to the pan -- it will foam up. Stir quickly.
Pour the butter mixture into the dry ingredients. Stir to combine -- the mixture will be loose and slightly crumbly.

Roll into balls the size of a walnut and place on the lined sheets, leaving space to spread. Flatten slightly. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes until golden. Leave on the tray for 5 minutes -- they firm up as they cool.

items.cause: Too much golden syrup or butter, or balls placed too close.
items.fix: Leave at least 6cm between each. If the mixture seems very wet, add a spoonful of extra oats.

items.symptom: Biscuits are crispy rather than chewy
items.cause: Baked at too high a temperature, or over-baked.
items.fix: Keep to 160C. Check at 12 minutes. The centre should still look a little underdone when you pull them out.

content.text: Anzac biscuits are strongly associated with Australia and New Zealand, where they were made during the First World War to send to soldiers overseas. The absence of eggs and the use of golden syrup meant they survived long journeys without spoiling. They are now eaten year-round across both countries and are familiar in Britain through Australian food culture.
